ExplanationEN: Neurocysticercosis is one of the most common causes (if not the most common cause) of seizures in the world. This disease is occurring with in- creasing frequency in the United States. The proposed reasons include increased immigration and increased travel to endemic parts of the world, including regions of Central and South America, India, other parts of Asia, and sub- Saharan Africa. According to the CDC, up to 2% of seizure presentations in the emergency department in the United States are from neurocysticercosis. It is caused by ingesting the eggs of the tapeworm Taenia solium, most com- monly through fecally contaminated foods. Cysticercosis should be distin- guished from tapeworm, which is the intestinal manifestation of Taenia solium in- fection. Neurologic complications are the number-one manifestation of cysticercosis, with seizures accounting for 70% to 90% of these presentations.

ExplanationEN: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, peripheral, demyelinating disease that produces flaccid paralysis and hyporeflexia. Both plasmapheresis and intra- venous immune globulin (IVIG) are accepted treatments for GBS. Patients treated with plasmapheresis compared to supportive care alone show im- provement in rates of motor function, need for mechanical ventilation, and long- term disability. The pudendal nerve consists of the S2 through S4 nerve roots and is responsible for external anal sphincter tone and sensation. Its compression is responsible for the loss of bowel continence. The other red-flag symptoms include urinary retention with a post-void residual volume greater than 200 mL and saddle anesthesia.

ExplanationEN: This patient's likely underlying diagnosis is acute compartment syndrome sec- ondary to the diaphyseal tibial fracture. A delta compartment pressure of less than 30 mm Hg is concerning for acute compartment syndrome. Delta compartment pressure is calculated by subtracting the compartment pressure from the diastolic blood pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure). Which intervention is the most appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN: A felon is an infection within the fingertip pulp that requires drainage, preferably using a high lateral incision. There are multiple septae within the fingertip pulp, creating individualized compartments that must be incised and drained to treat the infection. Failure to break up all septae (ie, leaving ab- scess behind) leads to recurrence of infection. Appropriate initial manage- ment is needed to avoid complications of an untreated or partially treated infection, such as osteomyelitis and flexor tenosynovitis. A high lateral incision (just volar to the fingernail) minimizes risk of injuring the digital artery, nerve, and volar fat pad. For the thumb and small finger, a single incision is made along the ra- dial aspect of the fingertip; for the index, middle, and ring fingers, a sin- gle incision is made along the ulnar aspect of the fingertip to preserve the ability to pinch. A through and through incision may be performed if it is unclear whether all of the septae have been broken up utilizing only a single incision. Treatment of felon also includes antibiotics covering for Staphylococcus au- reus (most common organism) and Streptococcus, as appropriate; con- sider MRSA coverage as indicated. Additionally, ensure appropriate follow-up (ideally within 72 hours) for a wound check.

ExplanationEN: This patient's presentation is consistent with dermatomyositis, which should ini- tially be treated with glucocorticoids. Patients with dermatomyositis present with proximal muscle weakness and cutaneous manifestations. Cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis include Gottron papules over the interpha- langeal and metacarpophalangeal joints; erythema over the joints (Gottron sign); heliotrope eruption (periorbital skin erythema without edema); and areas of violaceous erythema on the head, neck, upper ex- tremities, and upper chest. The areas of violaceous erythema are typically pru- ritic. The initial treatment for the muscle weakness in dermatomyositis is gluco- corticoids. Photoprotection, antipruritic agents, and topical corticosteroids or cal- cineurin inhibitors are used to treat cutaneous manifestations. Methotrexate and antimalarial drugs can also be used as second-line agents.

ExplanationEN: Rhabdomyosarcomas are of soft-tissue origin and are the most common childhood soft-tissue sarcoma (approximately 4.5 cases per 1 million children and adolescents per year). The presentation of rhabdomyosarcoma is vari- able, as these may occur at any site. A 14-year-old boy presents after developing a limp while playing in a week-long
soccer tournament. He endorses left knee pain, but he denies any falls or trauma
during the games. His symptoms are exacerbated by running and improved with
rest. On examination, he has full range of motion of the left knee with normal
strength. There is no effusion, but there is point tenderness over the tibial
tuberosity. His gait is currently normal and symmetric. X-rays of the knee show
an open apophysis of the tibial tuberosity without widening.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN: This patient has apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity, also known as Osgood- Schlatter disease. The apophysis is the attachment point between tendon and bone and is the weakest part of the bone-muscle-tendon unit. Apophysitis is the result of a traction injury to the apophysis, either from overuse or trauma. Risk factors for developing tibial tuberosity apophysitis include male sex, repetitive jumping and running activities, and periods of rapid growth. X-rays may be normal or may show mild fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity. Apophysitis is a self-limited condition that resolves at the time of skeletal maturity.

A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1-day history of painful rash on her arm.
She recently traveled to the Florida Keys for a SCUBA diving vacation. Her vital
signs include BP 108/70, P 83, R 16, and T 37°C (98.6°F). On examination, there
is a tender, erythematous 5-cm lesion on her forearm, with a necrotic center and
several hemorrhagic bullae.
Which medication is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
ExplanationEN: This patient likely has cellulitis secondary to Vibrio vulnificus, which should be treated with doxycycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftazidime). V. vulnificus is a naturally occurring gram-negative bac- terium that can be found along the warm coastal waters of the United States. It can be transmitted through ingestion of raw or undercooked shell- fish or from direct wound exposure to warm saltwater or brackish water. Rapidly progressive cellulitic skin changes with necrosis and skin bullae can develop from both routes of infection. Rapid treatment with antibiotics, supportive care, and surgical wound debridement is necessary, as mor- tality rates may reach 50% in patients with primary Vibrio septicemia and 15% in patients with primary Vibrio wound infections.

ExplanationEN: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of purulent skin and soft-tissue infections, such as cutaneous abscesses. ExplanationEN: Allopurinol has been strongly associated with the development of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). These disease processes are most commonly induced by medications and are differentiated by the amount of total body surface area (TBSA) undergoing skin de- tachment. In the majority of cases of SJS, SJS/TEN, and TEN, there is mucous membrane involvement (eg, ocular, oral, or genital involvement). SJS/TEN typically starts anywhere from 4 days to within 8 weeks of starting an associated medication. Other drugs commonly implicated in SJS/TEN are aromatic antiseizure medications, antibacterial sulfonamides, and oxi- cam NSAIDs.

The time to onset following the last alcoholic drink varies based on the patient's tolerance, but the first symptoms often appear within 6 to 12 hours. Symptoms may depend on how heavily the patient was previously drink- ing. The diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal requires at least two of the following symp- toms: autonomic hyperactivity (including tachycardia and hyperten- sion); hand tremor; insomnia; nausea or vomiting; transient visual, tac- tical, or auditory hallucinations or illusions; psychomotor agitation; anxiety; or grand mal seizures. Symptoms frequently worsen in patients with prior episodes of withdrawal. Symptoms generally proceed from autonomic hyperactivity to hallucinations to seizures to delirium tremens. Treatment is with benzodiazepines, frequently lo- razepam, diazepam, or chlordiazepoxide. Patients may also require thi- 2 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 807 of 974 amine and multivitamin supplementation  secondary  to  nutritional deficiencies.

History components that can aid in the diagnosis of thyroid storm include history of weight loss, known hyperthyroidism, or thyroid supplementation with levothyroxine. The Butch and Wartofsky Point Scale can help to diagnose thyroid storm based on clinical findings. This patient would have a score highly suggestive of thyroid storm. Treatment is a multistep process, consisting initially of supportive care, followed by beta blockade (usually propranolol or esmolol), inhibition of thyroid hor- mone synthesis with methimazole or propylthiouracil, inhibition of thyroid hormone release with iodine-containing solutions, and finally, prevention of conversion of T4 to T3 with hydrocortisone.

What medication is most likely the cause of her symptoms?
ExplanationEN: When taken with alcohol, metronidazole can result in a disulfiram-like reaction. Classically, disulfiram is associated with a disulfiram reaction. Disulfiram results in a hypersensitivity to alcohol by blocking aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), resulting in the accumulation of acetaldehyde. The consumption of alcohol while taking disulfiram causes the following symptoms: nausea, vomiting, flushing, headache, chest pain, palpitations, and di- aphoresis; in severe cases, confusion, hypotension, dysrhythmia, or seizure can occur. A disulfiram-like reaction can occur when alcohol is consumed with the presence of certain medications such as metronidazole, chloram- phenicol, griseofulvin, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, and certain cephalosporins. If prescribing these medications, it is important to counsel patients to avoid alcohol; if they currently are struggling with alcohol abuse, a different medication should be prescribed.

ExplanationEN: Agitated and violent patients who fail verbal de-escalation attempts may require chemical and physical restraints with the goal of minimizing harm to the patient and staff in the emergency department. ExplanationEN: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare but potentially fatal reaction associated with the use of antipsychotic medications. Any an- tipsychotic agent can lead to this condition. However, high potency first-genera- tion antipsychotics such as haloperidol carry the highest risk. Symptoms typically develop over days to weeks following initiation or dose increase of an- tipsychotic agents but can occur after single use or stable doses of medication. Higher-dose antipsychotic therapy is also a risk factor. Classic symptoms include altered  mental  status,  significant  hyperthermia,  dysautonomia, bradyreflexia, and muscle rigidity. Mortality can be as high as 10% to 20% and is attributed to dysautonomia and systemic complications including dehy- 2 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 835 of 974 dration, rhabdomyolysis, hepatic and renal failure, arrhythmia, my- ocardial infarction, and DIC. Treatment primarily involves cessation of the offending agent and support- ive care with rapid cooling, fluids, electrolyte repletion, and benzodi- azepines to decrease agitation and muscle tone. Intubation and paralysis may be required in severe cases. Distinguishing NMS from other toxidromes can be chal- lenging, but focusing on clinical context, timeline, drug history, and motor examina- tion is helpful in making the diagnosis.

ExplanationEN: Delusional disorder is divided into several subtypes based on the theme of the false belief. Subtypes include erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, per- secutory, somatic, mixed, and unspecified. Persecutory delusions are the most common type, involving the belief that one is being conspired against, spied on, harassed, or harmed in some way. Patients with this subtype of delusion may be angry towards those they believe are hurting them, may repeatedly pursue legal action, or may be subject to litigation as a result of independent actions taken to right the perceived injustice. CorrectAnswer: Obtain a set of vital signs
ExplanationEN: Although psychosis is a common feature of many psychiatric disorders, this condition can also be a symptom of an underlying medical condi- tion. Vital signs along with a thorough history and examination are key to differentiating medical etiologies from purely psychiatric causes. Findings that suggest an underlying medical etiology include abnormal vital signs or physical examination, non-auditory hallucinations, a history of substance abuse, or an acute change in mental status in a patient who lacks personal or family history of psychiatric disease. Abnormal vital signs can indicate underlying thyrotoxicosis, drug intox- ication, infection, or hypoxia, which should be addressed early in the patient assessment. Other medical causes of psychosis include metabolic disturbances such as glucose or electrolyte abnormalities, poisoning or medication toxic- ity, and CNS disorders including seizures, stroke, tumors, and autoim- mune conditions. The medical workup required for clearance depends on the clinical examination and history but should first start with vital signs and basic eval- uation of airway, breathing, and circulation.

vitals signs include BP 130/95, P 110, R 10, and T 37°C (98.6°F).
Which finding should raise suspicion of anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor en-
cephalitis as the underlying etiology of this patient's psychosis?
ExplanationEN: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is an in- creasingly recognized form of autoimmune encephalitis since its discov- ery in 2007 and is important to consider as a cause of new-onset psy- chosis. This illness impacts young female patients more than other groups and typically manifests as a nonspecific viral-like prodrome followed by neu- ropsychiatric symptoms weeks later. Most patients are younger than 40 years at initial presentation, with 37% of patients being younger than 18. Psychiatric symptoms frequently drive the initial presentation to health care settings and in- clude delusions, hallucinations, agitation, insomnia, mania, paranoia, or disorganized thinking. Symptoms can be more behavioral in young children. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis can initially be difficult to distinguish from other psychi- atric disorders, but the presence of motor abnormalities should prompt further in- vestigation. Most patients develop movement disorders during their ill- ness, and these can be an initial symptom, especially in younger pa- tients. Oro-lingual-facial dyskinesias are most characteristic, but patients can also have chorea, dystonia, rigidity, catatonia, bradykinesia, or stereotypies. If the condition is untreated, patients often develop language and memory dys- function, seizures, autonomic dysfunction, hypoventilation, and a de- pressed level of consciousness requiring ICU-level care. Diagnosis is made by finding antibodies to the NMDA receptor in serum or CSF, with CSF testing being the most sensitive. Treatment involves immunotherapy and should not wait for confirmation of diagnosis; con- firmation takes weeks, and early treatment improves outcomes. Recovery typically is slow, but about 80% of patients improve with treatment. Be careful with antipsy- chotic medications in these patients because they tend to be intolerant to an- tipsychotics and can develop clinical symptoms suggestive of neurolep- tic malignant syndrome after exposure.

A 16-year-old girl with no medical history presents after she collapsed at home.
She reports feeling generally weak and nauseous for several weeks. She denies
fevers or pain. Her mother says that she has always been a picky eater but re-
cently has been vomiting after meals. On examination, she has no abdominal ten-
derness. She appears malnourished and has soft, fine hair on her face and back
and calluses on the knuckles of her right hand. The patient believes she is over-
weight. Her vital signs are BP 80/50, P 45, R 18, and T 36.5°C (97.7°F); SpO  is
95% on room air.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN: This patient has anorexia nervosa, which is characterized by abnormally low body weight, a distorted perception of body weight and shape, fear of gaining weight, and persistent behavior to prevent weight gain. There are two subtypes: restrictive (the stereotypical form wherein patients re- strict caloric intake and often engage in excessive exercise) and binge- eating/purging (wherein patients engage in recurrent episodes of purg- ing behavior to avoid weight gain). Purging behaviors can involve self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic abuse, and even failure to take insulin in a patient with diabetes. This patient demonstrates characteristics of the binge-purge subtype of anorexia nervosa. She has several physical signs of an eating disorder: she is very thin and has lanugo (soft, fine hair on the body) and Russell sign (calluses on the knuckles, which can result from self-induced vomiting). Other clinical clues for patients with purge-type eating disorders include sialadenosis (which 2 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 850 of 974 is most commonly bilateral and in the parotid glands) and dental ero- sion and hoarseness from repeated exposure to stomach acid.

ity is likely to be present?
ExplanationEN: Although patients with restrictive eating disorders typically have normal electrolyte levels and acid-base status, patients with purge-type eating disorders (bu- limia and the binge-purge subtype of anorexia) often have electrolyte and acid-base disturbances. The types of abnormalities seen depend on the type of purging behavior. Repetitive vomiting can cause hypochloremic, hy- pokalemic metabolic alkalosis. More than 40% of patients who purge by vom- iting twice a day or more are hypokalemic. On ECG, evidence of severe hy- pokalemia can manifest as U-waves, T-wave inversion, ST-segment de- pression, and prolonged QT interval. Repleting the potassium typically re- solves ECG abnormalities.

A 16-year-old girl with no past medical history presents after she collapsed at
home. She reports feeling generally weak and nauseous for several weeks. She
denies fevers or pain. She choked a few months ago; since then, she has been
scared to ingest anything solid and overall avoids eating in general. Her mother
is concerned because she has been losing weight and passed out tonight for the
first time. She appears malnourished and recognizes she is thin. Her vital signs
are BP 80/50, P 48 (while asleep), R 18, and T 36.5°C (97.7°F); SpO  is 95% on
room air. The mother is concerned the patient may be depressed. On evaluation,
a superior pubic ramus fracture is diagnosed.
What is an indication for hospitalization in this patient?

Options.text: Superior pubic ramus fracture with osteopenia

ExplanationEN: This patient has avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) trig- gered by a traumatic experience with eating. Subsequent food avoidance can result in rapid weight loss and medical instability in these patients. Severe malnu- trition in restrictive eating disorders, which include anorexia nervosa and ARFID, can lead to cardiovascular complications, which are among the leading causes of death in these patients. Along with loss of skeletal muscle, car- diac muscle mass is decreased. This leads to decreased contractility and cardiac out- put and in some cases can cause mitral valve prolapse. Vagal tone also is increased to conserve energy. As a result, malnourished patients may present with hypoten- sion, bradycardia, and orthostasis. Judicious intravenous fluid use is needed to avoid precipitation of pulmonary edema. Current recommenda- tions by both the American Psychiatric Association and the Society of Adolescent Medicine suggest hospitalization of patients with restrictive eating disor- ders who have cardiac manifestations of disease including significant bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension, and syncope.

A 16-year-old girl with no past medical history presents after she collapsed at
home. She reports feeling generally weak and nauseous for several weeks. She
denies fevers or pain. On examination, she has no abdominal tenderness. Her
weight is normal. Her mother reports she has been compulsively eating soil over
the past few months and is wondering why she has these cravings.
What element of history is associated with the development of pica?
ExplanationEN: Pica is a clinical diagnosis made when a patient persistently eats sub- stances that are not food and are of no nutritional value for a period of over 1 month. When this behavior involves ingestion of earth (soil, clay, etc.), it is referred to as geophagia and can lead to bacterial, fungal, and helminth infections and lead poisoning, among other complications. The etiology of pica is unknown. Pica often occurs in patients with mental health disorders such as autism, schizophrenia, and intellectual disability. It is also associ- ated with medical conditions including anemia, nutritional deficiency, and pregnancy. Patients diagnosed with pica should be evaluated for these underlying medical conditions and also for potential complications of ingestions, including bowel obstruction, electrolyte disturbance, ane- mia, toxins, or infections, depending on the substance consumed.

to thrive?
ExplanationEN: Multiple triggers can lead to failure to thrive (FTT), and patients may present with a variety of physical and mental manifestations. FTT is often described as a dis- order of weight loss, decreased appetite, poor nutrition, and inactivity, per the National Institute of Aging. Additionally, FTT can be accompanied by dehy- dration, depression, impaired immune function, and low cholesterol. Weight loss, malnutrition, and inactivity are also features of frailty. This term is of- ten used in pediatrics to describe those patients who do not gain weight, subse- quently suffering cognitive, depressive, and developmental effects. The key fea- ture that must be present to diagnose FTT is frailty (weight loss, malnu- trition, and physical inactivity). Significant weight loss is defined as loss of 5% of body weight over a 6 to 12 month period. It is important to obtain a careful history and physical examination and to do a broad evaluation to look for causes and complications of FTT. Changes in social support systems can pre- cipitate FTT.

A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, with a history of gestational diabetes,
presents 14 weeks after vaginal delivery complaining of inability to sleep. Further
history reveals that she has a history of depression, and over the past 4 weeks,
she has also experienced difficulty concentrating, fatigue, loss of appetite, and in-
creasing guilt due to her lack of interest in taking care of her infant. She is afraid
because she has had increasing thoughts about wanting to go to sleep and not
wake up.
What factor places this patient at greatest risk of postpartum depression?
ExplanationEN: Postpartum depression has been shown to affect approximately 10% of patients in the postpartum period up to 12 months after delivery. Postpartum depression is defined as depression within the first 12 months of childbirth with at least 5 symptoms of major depression disorder present for at least 2 weeks. A prepregnancy history of depression and mood disorder have been found to have the largest effect on incidence of postpartum depression. Patients with a history of depression have a twofold increased risk of developing post- partum depression compared with those with no history of depression or mood 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 871 of 974 disorder. Other risk factors that contribute to the development of postpartum de- pression are increased stress in the postpartum period (such as marital conflict or being a single parent with poor social or financial support), young age (less than 25 years), health difficulties during pregnancy, multiparity, difficulty breastfeeding, and infant sleep disturbance.

A 27-year-old woman is brought in by EMS after seizure-like activity. The patient
was presenting in court when she fell to the ground and had rhythmic shaking of
all of her extremities, pelvic thrusting, and turning of her head side to side for 10
minutes. EMS reports that her eyes were closed too tightly to assess for gaze de-
viation. The seizure stopped after she was put in the ambulance, and she was im-
mediately alert and oriented with a GCS score of 15. On examination, the patient
is well appearing, her pupils are 3 mm bilaterally, and her oropharynx is clear.
Her full neurological examination is unremarkable. Her BMP is all within normal
limits. A pregnancy test result is negative, and an ECG reveals sinus rhythm at a
rate of 80 bpm.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
ExplanationEN: Nonepileptiform seizure, historically referred to as pseudoseizure or psychogenic seizure, is seizure-like activity without associated abnor- mal CNS activity. The diagnosis of nonepileptiform seizure can be suspected with a thorough history and examination and witness information of the seizure activity. However, this information should be coupled with EEG with video monitoring to make the most accurate diagnosis. This case highlights some of the features that may be seen in nonepileptiform seizure activity, such as lack of a postictal period, lack of intraoral trauma, lack of incontinence, and absence of anion gap (from the elevated LDH that can be associated with seizure) on laboratory findings, along with purposeful eye closing during the seizure-like activity and association with a stressful event. Other findings that are seen in nonepileptiform seizures include pelvic thrusting, asynchronous movements, moving the head from side to side, and lack of tachycardia and cyanosis during the seizure. Nonepileptiform seizures typically are witnessed and can be associated with stress. A patient sus- pected to have had a nonepileptiform seizure should undergo the same diagnostic evaluation as is done for a typical seizure (neuroimaging, labs, ECG) to assure there is no other organic underlying cause.

What is the most likely etiology of the patient's recurrent presentations of

ExplanationEN: Exogenous insulin administration would explain the recurrent episodes of unexplained hypoglycemia with a C-peptide level less than 0.2 ng/mL. In hypoglycemia, the C-peptide level helps distinguish endogenous versus exoge- nous hyperinsulinemia. Circulating exogenous insulin suppresses C-peptide pro- duction. This test can be useful when caregiver-fabricated illness (Munchausen syn- drome by proxy) is being considered as a possible etiology of unexplained hypo- glycemia in a child. Caregiver-fabricated illness is very difficult to diagnose be- cause there is no classic presentation. It should be considered when a child presents frequently for medical intervention (often to different providers and hospitals), diagnostic results do not match the clinical picture, and symptoms do not follow expected treatment courses (eg, an episode of hypoglycemia does not correct as expected). The perpetrator is often doting and affable, and they may be overly eager for invasive proce- dures for the child. Another clue is cessation of the victim's acute symp- toms when the perpetrator is absent. This case is an example of produced illness, wherein the parent creates illness in the child using various methods to create sickness, such as administering inappropriate medication, injecting feces into central lines, or using techniques of asphyxiation. Simulated illness is the other, less harmful technique that a parent suffering from 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 887 of 974 caregiver-fabricated illness may employ, avoiding direct harm to the child. Examples include adding blood to a urine specimen, falsifying symptoms, or altering laboratory results. This is a form of child abuse and can be life threatening. Child Protective Services must be involved to protect the vic- tim, in addition to psychiatric evaluation for the perpetrator suffering from caregiver-fabricated illness.

A 45-year-old man presents for left forearm pain. The patient has a history of
stimulant use disorder and reports intravenous injection of methamphetamine.
He reports pain, redness, and swelling of his forearm at the injection site for 3
days. His vital signs on arrival are BP 112/74, P 72, R 18, and T 37.0°C (98.6°F);
SpO  is 96% on room air. On examination, his left antecubital fossa shows ery-
thema, which is warm to touch and tender to palpation. A POCUS demonstrates
a cutaneous abscess that measures 0.5 cm by 0.5 cm.
What is the correct antibiotic choice?
ExplanationEN: Intravenous drug use is a risk factor for developing cellulitis and ab- scess of the skin and soft tissues. In addition to incision and drainage of the cutaneous abscess, antibiotics are recommended for the treatment of purulent SSTIs. Appropriate antibiotics for the treatment of purulent SSTI in- clude  linezolid,  clindamycin,  doxycycline,  daptomycin, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, and vancomycin. Common microbes in this patient population include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), streptococcal species, and anaerobic organisms. Both streptococcal species and anaerobic organisms are found in the oral cavity. It is hypothesized that the licking of needles is why these microbes are more commonly identified in skin and soft-tissue infections (SSTIs) of injection drug users compared to non-injection drug users. Given that this patient does not have evidence of systemic infection and is clinically well appearing, starting the patient on an oral antibiotic like doxycycline for outpatient management of the purulent SSTI is the most appropriate treatment strategy.

headache. There is no history of trauma. Her vital signs are BP 130/80, P 120, R
24, and T 36.9°C (98.4°F); SpO  is 100% on room air. Her blood glucose level is
98 mg/dL. A carbon monoxide level is measured at 13%.
What is the best next step for treatment?
ExplanationEN: Carbon monoxide (CO) binds to Hgb with a significantly (200 times) greater affinity than oxygen, thus decreasing the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Treatment for CO poisoning is to promote removal of the CO from Hgb, enabling oxygen to again bind and oxygenate tissues. Supplemental 100% oxy- gen works to decrease the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin to 1 to 2 hours from 4 to 5 hours in room-air conditions. Given high clinical suspicion for CO poisoning and that this patient is experiencing symptoms after exposure to a 2 9/20/26, 1:18 AM PEER for Physicians - Case Series 2026-1 — Answered  Page 897 of 974 house fire, 100% supplemental oxygen via a nonrebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min should be initiated immediately. is measured at 23%. Initial fetal monitoring is reassuring.

ExplanationEN: Hyperbaric oxygen is indicated for patients who demonstrate end-organ damage from ischemia associated with carbon monoxide (CO) poison- ing. Hyperbaric oxygen decreases the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin to 20 to 40 minutes and should be considered in severe cases of CO poisoning. A 37-year-old woman with a history of tuberculosis presents with tonic-clonic
seizure activity. She is reportedly 22 weeks' pregnant. There is no known history
of trauma, and she was acting normally 3 hours prior to the arrival of EMS. She
was found with an empty prescription pill bottle. Out-of-hospital, she received
diazepam 4 mg IV with no change in her seizure activity. On arrival, she has
tonic-clonic seizure activity. Her vital signs are BP 110/70, P 120, R 22, and T
36.8°C (98.2°F); SpO  is 94% on nonrebreather mask. Her glucose level is 80
mg/dL. Given persistent continued seizure activity, she is given additional benzo-
diazepine IV.
What is the most likely cause of her refractory seizure?
ExplanationEN: Isoniazid (INH) is an antimicrobial used to treat active or latent tuberculosis. INH is rapidly absorbed, reaching peak serum concentrations within 30 minutes to 2 hours after ingestion. INH increases elimination of pyridoxine and in- hibits pyridoxine phosphokinase. Pyridoxine phosphokinase metabolizes pyri- doxine to pyridoxal 5'-phospheate, a required cofactor of glutamic acid decarboxy- lase required to convert glutamate — a stimulatory neurotransmitter — to GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Inhibition of pyridoxine phosphoki- nase results in GABA deficiency, leading to seizure activity. This patient has a history of tuberculosis and is pregnant. Given her presentation with refractory seizures, we can presume the empty bottle contained INH. An acute overdose of INH would lead to inhibition of pyridoxine phosphokinase, decreased levels of GABA, and increased seizure activity. Pregnancy is associated with increased risk of INH toxicity. As such, INH is often not used in pregnant patients unless the benefit of use outweighs the risk.

finding an empty bottle of “anemia pills'' near the patient. The patient's vital

wall crepitus. Her laboratory results are currently pending.
Which imaging modality is preferred in the management of this patient?
ExplanationEN: This patient's presentation is concerning for an iron ingestion given the “anemia pills” found nearby. Abdominal x-ray is recommended in acute iron inges- tions. Iron tablets are radiopaque, and large overdoses of tablets will appear within the GI tract. A positive finding on x-ray will help facilitate management with GI decontamination, including nasogastric lavage or whole bowel irrigation if indicated. The decision for GI decontamination should be made in concert with a specialist in medical toxicology. Notably, some preparations of iron, such as liquid formulations or chewable tablets, are generally not radiopaque. Thus, the absence of radiopaque tablets does not exclude iron toxicity. Findings may be negative secondary to the formulation of iron prod- uct ingested or delayed presentation after ingestion.

ExplanationEN: Given the presence of a significant anion gap, metabolic acidosis, and kidney injury, ethylene glycol toxicity is the most likely diagnosis. When ingested, ethylene glycol can also cause inebriation with similar findings to ethanol intoxication. This diagnosis must be recognized in a timely manner and treated promptly. Otherwise, it can re- sult in life-threatening acidemia and renal failure.

ExplanationEN: A sodium bicarbonate infusion is considered the antidote for salicylate toxicity. This antidote is generally recommended when the salicylate con- centration is >30 mg/dL. Sodium bicarbonate facilitates the renal elimina- tion of salicylates from the vascular compartment via a mechanism known as ion trapping. patient appears anxious, alert, and oriented x 3; mild bilateral hand tremor is
present. His last drink of alcohol was 1 day ago. In the emergency department,
the patient has a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
Which medication should be administered?
ExplanationEN: Lorazepam has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent alcohol with- drawal seizures. In a randomized, double-blinded study, 2 mg of intravenous lo- razepam was shown to reduce the risk of recurrent seizure from 24% to 3% during a 6-hour observation period in the emergency department. It was also shown to re- duce the need for hospital admission from 42% in the placebo group to 29% in the lorazepam group. The etiology of seizure in the setting of alcohol withdrawal is related to downregula- tion of the gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor secondary to chronic alcohol exposure and a compensatory upregulation of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. Therefore, cessation of alcohol use causes increased excitatory activity, re- sulting in seizures that are seen in alcohol withdrawal. Benzodiazepines coun- teract the underlying mechanism that leads to alcohol withdrawal seizures by increasing the GABAergic activity.

A 24-year-old man presents for anxiety and irritability. He endorses fatigue and
subjective fevers. He uses intravenous heroin daily. His vital signs on arrival are
BP 100/60, P 120, R 20, and T 39.0°C (102.2°F); SpO  is 98% on room air. On
examination, the patient is ill appearing, and there is a II/VI systolic murmur in
the lower left sternal border.
What diagnostic test should be ordered?
ExplanationEN: A fever in a patient with a history of intravenous drug use (IVDU) warrants immedi- ate concern. The differential diagnosis for IVDU and fever includes diag- noses such as spinal epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, and infective endocarditis (IE). Given the risk of severe infection, any patient with a fever and history of IVDU should be thoroughly evaluated to identify the source of infection. In this case, the presence of the murmur increases the in- dex of suspicion for infective endocarditis. In patients with a fever and his- tory of IVDU, nearly 15% are diagnosed with IE. Collecting at least three sets of blood cultures increases the sensitivity of detecting bacteremia. Three sets of blood cultures demonstrates organisms in 98% of cases, compared to 90% when two sets of blood cultures are collected. This is critical because blood culture positivity is one of the major criteria in the modified Duke criteria for diagnosis of IE.

(98.6°F); SpO  is 98% on room air. He is well appearing and comfortable, and
the remainder of his examination is unremarkable.
What medication will precipitate opioid withdrawal?
ExplanationEN: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist of the mu-opioid receptor. It is used in the treat- ment of opioid withdrawal and in medication-assisted treatment of opioid use dis- order. Administration of buprenorphine to patients receiving methadone maintenance therapy can precipitate withdrawal. Buprenorphine has a high binding affinity for the mu-opioid receptor, 1,000 times greater than morphine. As a result, therapeutic doses of buprenorphine can displace full opioid ago- nists like methadone from the mu-opioid receptor and can precipitate opi- oid withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients. Given the long half-life of methadone, it is generally recommended that at least 72 hours since the last dose of methadone should pass before buprenorphine treatment is considered.

Question: A 25-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain that has persisted for 3 days. The pain is associated with some shortness of breath. She denies fevers, cough, chills, nausea, and vomiting. She appears in mild distress. Vital signs on arrival are BP 115/75, P 110, R 18, and T 36.7°C (98.0°F); SpO2 is 97% on room air. On examination, her lungs are clear to auscultation, her heart is tachycardic with regular rhythm, and there are no murmurs. Her abdomen is soft and nontender, and her extremities are without swelling and are warm and well perfused. Which additional history or physical examination component should raise the most suspicion for pulmonary embolism?

Options.text: History of Hodgkin lymphoma, in remission 2 years
Right ankle open reduction internal fixation 3 months ago

ExplanationEN: There are several important factors in history that should raise suspicion for venous thromboembolism (VTE). Some of the risk factors include active cancer, surgery or trauma within the last 4 weeks, estrogen use, prior venous thromboembolism, age older than 50 years, and BMI greater than 35 kg/m². The risk increases with increasing BMI and with each year of life over 50 years. The risk of development of pulmonary embolism is nearly sixfold higher among women with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m². This risk factor is not included in many decision-making tools for VTE; therefore, it is important to remember.
ExplanationAR: عوامل خطر الخثار الوريدي (VTE) تشمل: السرطان النشط، الجراحة أو الرضح خلال 4 أسابيع، الإستروجين، VTE سابق، العمر >50، ومؤشر كتلة الجسم >35. السمنة ترفع خطر الانصمام الرئوي (PE) نحو 6 أضعاف عبر الركود الوريدي وفرط التخثر. هذه العلامة لا توجد في معظم أدوات القرار، لذا يجب تذكرها.

Lungs clear, heart tachycardic. An ECG is performed immediately. What ECG finding would be the most specific for pulmonary embolism?

Options.text: Sinus tachycardia with dominant R wave in V1
T-wave inversion in inferior and right precordial leads

CorrectAnswer: T-wave inversion in inferior and right precordial leads
ExplanationEN: ECG changes found with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) include any changes that would be seen in acute pulmonary hypertension. T-wave inversions are typically associated with ACS; however, there are a few cases where acute PE should be higher on the differential. Studies have shown that simultaneous T-wave inversions in the inferior (II, III, aVF) and right precordial (V1-V4) leads are the most specific finding in favor of PE. One study showed a specificity of 99%. The cause of T-wave inversions in acute PE is not completely understood but is thought to involve the development of acute cor pulmonale due to right ventricular overload, leading to ischemia of the right ventricle.
ExplanationAR: أكثر علامة ECG نوعية للانصمام الرئوي هي انقلاب موجة T المتزامن في الخيوط السفلية (II, III, aVF) والصدريّة اليمنى (V1-V4)، بخصوصية تصل 99%. الآلية: القلب الرئوي الحاد (acute cor pulmonale) من تحميل البطين الأيمن ونقص ترويته.

Question: A 25-year-old woman with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, clear lungs, tachycardia. A D-dimer test is ordered. What further piece of history would raise suspicion for a falsely elevated D-dimer level?
ExplanationEN: D-dimer is one of the protein fragments created when blood clots break down. In liver disease, there is decreased clearance of these protein fragments, leading to elevated D-dimer levels. D-dimer levels can also be elevated in the following circumstances: pregnancy, kidney disease, malignancy, trauma, surgical procedure in the previous week, rheumatoid arthritis, infection, and age older than 70 years. Warfarin can actually cause D-dimer levels to be falsely lowered.
ExplanationAR: أمراض الكبد تُقلل تصفية شظايا D-dimer في الدم → ارتفاع كاذب في قيمته. أسباب أخرى: الحمل، أمراض الكلى، الأورام، الرضح، الجراحة الحديثة، التهاب المفاصل الروماتويدي، العدوى، والعمر >70. الوارفارين قد يخفض D-dimer كاذبًا.

Question: A 25-year-old woman at a rural hospital with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, BP 86/62, P 120, R 24, SpO2 90%. CT shows saddle PE with pulmonary infarct. After 1-L fluid bolus, patient worsens: BP 70/54, P 120, SpO2 88% on 6-L NC, drowsy. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Administer tPA and start the patient on a norepinephrine infusion
Start an epinephrine infusion and begin a heparin bolus, followed by a drip

CorrectAnswer: Administer tPA and start the patient on a norepinephrine infusion
ExplanationEN: Pulmonary embolism (PE) can be classified into three categories based on severity: massive, submassive, and less severe. Patients with a massive PE have a systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mm Hg for more than 15 minutes. Evidence suggests that fibrinolysis should be given or seriously considered in all patients with any of the following: cardiac arrest, hypotension, or respiratory failure. Alteplase for PE in the non-cardiac arrest setting is 100 mg IV over 2 hours. Norepinephrine is the recommended vasopressor. Excess preload in massive PE can exacerbate right ventricular dilation.
ExplanationAR: الانصمام الرئوي الضخم (massive PE) مع هبوط ضغط مستمر يتطلب حالًا للـ fibrin (alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h) + دعم وعائي بالنورإبينفرين. الإكثار من السوائل قد يزيد تمدد البطين الأيمن ويُفاقم الحالة.

Question: A 60-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, and obesity presents with chest pain beginning 2 hours ago. ECG shows no ST elevation. What diagnostic study is needed to help differentiate non-ST elevation infarction from unstable angina?
ExplanationEN: A rise in troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile is diagnostic for acute myocardial ischemia in patients with symptoms consistent with ACS. If the troponin is normal, then unstable angina is possible. The best way to differentiate NSTEMI from unstable angina is serum troponin.

Question: A 60-year-old man with NSTEMI (troponin 0.30 ng/mL) is given aspirin. What other emergency department intervention has been shown to improve mortality in patients like this one?
ExplanationEN: In addition to aspirin, clopidogrel should be given to patients with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in the emergency department. The CURE trial found that dual-antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) decreased cardiovascular death and nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke when compared to aspirin alone.

Question: A 60-year-old man with NSTEMI is to receive clopidogrel. What information must be obtained from the cardiologist before giving clopidogrel?

Options.text: Possibility of coronary artery bypass graft

CorrectAnswer: Possibility of coronary artery bypass graft
ExplanationEN: It is important to know if this patient may require a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) prior to giving clopidogrel. Clopidogrel has been proven to improve mortality in acute myocardial ischemia. However, clopidogrel increases bleeding risk and should not be given if there is a possibility of the patient undergoing a CABG. The loading dose of clopidogrel is 300 mg.

Question: A 60-year-old man with NSTEMI on aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin drip develops BP 80/40, P 180, wide-complex regular tachycardia. What is the best next step?
ExplanationEN: This patient is in unstable ventricular tachycardia. The rhythm is wide-complex, regular, and fast. Because the patient's blood pressure is 80/40, he is considered unstable. The treatment for unstable ventricular tachycardia is synchronized cardioversion at 100 J. Defibrillation should only be done in pulseless VT or VF.

Question: An 8-year-old girl with viral infection, ECG diffuse PR depressions and ST elevations, CXR pulmonary fluid overload and dilated cardiac silhouette, BP 62/32. What is the best combination of medications?
ExplanationEN: This patient is suffering from cardiogenic shock in the setting of viral myocarditis. Vasopressor support will need to address two issues: inotropic support for cardiac output (CO) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Dobutamine has strong beta-1 receptor activity, which increases CO. Norepinephrine's strong alpha activity will increase the SVR.
ExplanationAR: الصدمة القلبية في التهاب العضلة القلبية الفيروسي تتطلب دعمًا مقويًا للقلب ودعمًا للمقاومة الوعائية. الدوبوتامين (β1) يزيد النتاج القلبي، والنورإبينفرين (α) يرفع SVR.

Question: A 34-year-old man with chest pressure, syncope, HR 32 with no P-QRS association, BP 85/42, recent camping in New England, annular rash. What is the most likely cause?
ExplanationEN: This patient is showing signs of acute cardiogenic shock from myocarditis with an associated third-degree heart block. The most likely diagnosis is Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted via Ixodes ticks. Cardiac complications occur in 10% of patients and typically occur 2-4 weeks after infection. The rash noted was most likely erythema migrans, which occurs in 90% of patients. Treatment is doxycycline.
ExplanationAR: داء لايم (Lyme disease) يسببه Borrelia burgdorferi عبر قراد Ixodes. يسبب حمامى مهاجرة (erythema migrans) في 90% ومضاعفات قلبية في 10% (قد تصل لحصار ثلاثي الدرجة). العلاج: doxycycline.

Question: A 65-year-old man in acute respiratory distress with CHF, bilateral pitting edema, reduced EF. What medication is contraindicated in this acute setting?
ExplanationEN: This patient is in cardiogenic shock with fluid overload and hypotension. Although beta-blockers are excellent agents for chronic and compensated heart failure, administering them to a patient in acute and decompensated heart failure, particularly one in shock, is contraindicated. The beta-blocker will cause negative inotropy and worsen the clinical condition.
ExplanationAR: حاصرات بيتا (beta-blockers) ممنوعة في فشل القلب الحاد اللا معاوض مع الصدمة لأنها تسبب تأثيرًا سلبيًا على الانقباض (negative inotropy) وتفاقم الحالة. مفيدة فقط في فشل القلب المعاوض المزمن.
ClinicalScenario: A 65-year-old man in acute respiratory distress with CHF, bilateral pitting edema, reduced EF. What medication is contraindicated in this acute setting?

Question: A 72-year-old woman with coxsackievirus infection in cardiogenic shock despite excellent critical care. Which intervention would be potentially the most beneficial?
ExplanationEN: Venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) has shown promise in studies for patients with cardiogenic shock. It effectively replaces the functions of the failing heart and lungs. The intra-aortic balloon pump has shown some success but randomized controlled trials have repeatedly failed to show improvement in patient-centered outcomes, including 30-day mortality.
ExplanationAR: ECMO الشرياني الوريدي (VA-ECMO) يستبدل وظائف القلب والرئتين الفاشلة وأظهر نتائج واعدة في الصدمة القلبية. البالون داخل الأبهر (IABP) لم يُثبت تحسنًا في نتائج المرضى أو وفيات 30 يومًا في التجارب العشوائية.
ClinicalScenario: A 72-year-old woman with coxsackievirus infection in cardiogenic shock despite excellent critical care. Which intervention would be potentially the most beneficial?

Question: A 57-year-old man with COPD and hypertension presents with left pleuritic chest pain, no air movement on left, decreased excursion, BP 93/60. What would be a late finding of the cause?
ExplanationEN: This patient has a tension pneumothorax. Although tracheal deviation is commonly taught as a finding in tension pneumothorax, it is extremely rare; when it does occur, it is a very late finding. Treatment is needle decompression followed by tube thoracostomy.
ExplanationAR: انحراف القصبة الهوائية (tracheal deviation) في استرواح الصدر الضاغط علامة نادرة ومتأخرة جدًا ولا يجب الاعتماد عليها للتشخيص. العلاج: تخفيف بالإبرة ثم أنبوب صدري.
ClinicalScenario: A 57-year-old man with COPD and hypertension presents with left pleuritic chest pain, no air movement on left, decreased excursion, BP 93/60. What would be a late finding of the cause?

Question: A 14-year-old boy with intermittent sharp chest pain after a choking event. CXR shows pneumomediastinum. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Consult ENT for foreign body removal

ExplanationEN: This patient has a spontaneous primary pneumomediastinum resulting from alveolar rupture due to increases in thoracic pressure. Treatment is directed at the underlying cause or precipitating event. Children with primary causes can often be observed in the emergency department and discharged if stable. The course is usually benign and resolves in 1 to 2 weeks.
ExplanationAR: استرواح المنصف الأولي العفوي ناتج عن تمزق الحويصلات بسبب ارتفاع الضغط الصدري. المسار حميد ويشفى تلقائيًا في 1-2 أسبوع؛ لذا يكفي مراقبة قصيرة ثم إخراج المريض إذا كان مستقرًا.
ClinicalScenario: A 14-year-old boy with intermittent sharp chest pain after a choking event. CXR shows pneumomediastinum. What is the best next step in management?

Question: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, sudden pleuritic chest pain after forceful emesis, BP 98/62, P 133, T 38.6°C, CXR subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinal widening, bilateral pleural effusions. What is the best next step?

Options.text: Consult cardiothoracic surgery for operative repair
Obtain a CT with contrast to confirm diagnosis

CorrectAnswer: Consult cardiothoracic surgery for operative repair
ExplanationEN: This patient has mediastinitis secondary to Boerhaave syndrome. Given the patient's clinical condition, history of symptoms occurring after forceful emesis, and chest x-ray findings, it is most reasonable to consult cardiothoracic surgery for emergent operative repair. Mortality is time dependent and nearly doubles within the first 12 hours.
ExplanationAR: متلازمة بورهاف (Boerhaave syndrome) مع التهاب المنصف (mediastinitis) والصدمة الإنتانية تتطلب إصلاحًا جراحيًا عاجلًا. الوفيات تتضاعف خلال 12 ساعة؛ لذا يجب عدم تأخير الجراحة للفحوصات التأكيدية.
ClinicalScenario: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, sudden pleuritic chest pain after forceful emesis, BP 98/62, P 133, T 38.6°C, CXR subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinal widening, bilateral pleural effusions. What is the best next step?

Question: A 23-year-old woman with 3 days of sharp chest pain worse with inspiration, recent URI and cough. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. What intervention is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Obtain a troponin level and bedside ultrasound

ExplanationEN: This patient has costochondritis, likely precipitated by coughing. ECG shows benign early repolarization: diffuse concave ST elevation without reciprocal changes, ST/T wave ratio less than 0.25 in lead V6, and absence of PR segment depression. Treatment is supportive care including oral NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and avoidance of exacerbating activities.
ExplanationAR: التهاب الغضروف الضلعي (costochondritis) مع إعادة استقطاب مبكرة حميدة على ECG (ارتفاع ST مقعر منتشر بدون تغييرات متبادلة). العلاج تحفظي: NSAIDs، acetaminophen، وتجنب الأنشطة المُفاقِمة.
ClinicalScenario: A 23-year-old woman with 3 days of sharp chest pain worse with inspiration, recent URI and cough. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. What intervention is the most appropriate next step?

Question: A 43-year-old man with sudden chest pain, diastolic decrescendo murmur, left eye ptosis, constriction of left pupil. What other finding would most likely be expected?
ExplanationEN: This patient has an aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta given findings of incomplete Horner syndrome and an aortic regurgitation murmur. Acute aortic regurgitation commonly manifests with left ventricular failure and pulmonary edema. Type A dissections are more likely to manifest with normotension or hypotension.
ExplanationAR: تسلخ الأبهر الصاعد (Type A) مع متلازمة هورنر جزئية ولغط قلس الأبهر. القلس الأبهري الحاد يؤدي إلى فشل البطين الأيسر ووذمة رئوية. التسلخ الصاعد غالبًا مع ضغط طبيعي أو منخفض.
ClinicalScenario: A 43-year-old man with sudden chest pain, diastolic decrescendo murmur, left eye ptosis, constriction of left pupil. What other finding would most likely be expected?

Question: A 43-year-old man with sudden chest pain, diastolic murmur, partial Horner syndrome, CXR widened mediastinum. What intervention is the most appropriate next step?

Options.text: Administer a nicardipine bolus and drip
Consult cardiothoracic surgery for surgical management

CorrectAnswer: Consult cardiothoracic surgery for surgical management
ExplanationEN: This patient has an ascending aortic dissection. Dissections involving the ascending aorta are managed with surgical and/or endovascular therapy in addition to pharmacologic agents. Definitive treatment is surgical. Pharmacologic management includes lowering the heart rate to approximately 60 bpm and systolic BP between 100 to 120; beta-blockers should be started before vasodilators.
ExplanationAR: تسلخ الأبهر الصاعد (Type A) يتطلب تدبيرًا جراحيًا عاجلًا. الدوائي: خفض معدل القلب إلى ~60 والضغط الانقباضي 100-120. حاصرات بيتا أولًا ثم الموسعات الوعائية (nicardipine).
ClinicalScenario: A 43-year-old man with sudden chest pain, diastolic murmur, partial Horner syndrome, CXR widened mediastinum. What intervention is the most appropriate next step?

Question: A 53-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia, 10 days of nonproductive cough. Started lisinopril 2 weeks ago. What is the appropriate next step?
ExplanationEN: ACE inhibitors are a well-known cause of nonproductive cough. The cough typically begins within a week of starting the medication but may begin up to 6 months later. Treatment is discontinuation of the ACE inhibitor. The cough generally resolves within 4 days of discontinuing the ACE inhibitor but may take up to a month.
ExplanationAR: مثبطات ACE تسبب سعالًا جافًا، يبدأ عادةً خلال أسبوع من البدء وقد يتأخر حتى 6 أشهر. العلاج: إيقاف الدواء؛ يتحسن السعال خلال 4 أيام إلى شهر.
ClinicalScenario: A 53-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia, 10 days of nonproductive cough. Started lisinopril 2 weeks ago. What is the appropriate next step?

Question: A 53-year-old man with productive cough, body aches, chills, wheezing. CXR normal. Discharged with primary care follow-up. What is the best treatment plan?

Options.text: Instruct the patient to stop taking lisinopril
Prescribe an albuterol inhaler plus 5 days of steroids

ExplanationEN: This patient has acute bronchitis based on the clinical picture. Although there is no evidence to support routine use of beta-agonists for acute bronchitis, they have been shown to lower symptom scores and lead to faster cough resolution in patients with evidence of airflow obstruction on examination (wheezing). Antibiotics and steroids are not beneficial.
ExplanationAR: التهاب الشعب الهوائية الحاد مع أزيز (wheezing): بخاخ الألبوتيرول (albuterol) يقلل شدة الأعراض ويسرّع شفاء السعال. المضادات الحيوية والستيرويدات غير مفيدة.
ClinicalScenario: A 53-year-old man with productive cough, body aches, chills, wheezing. CXR normal. Discharged with primary care follow-up. What is the best treatment plan?

Question: A 63-year-old woman with dry cough for 20 days, congestion, myalgias, babysitting a 3-month-old grandchild with cough. Subconjunctival hemorrhage. What other diagnostic test would be helpful?
ExplanationEN: This patient's presentation is concerning for Bordetella pertussis infection. The patient has had a cough for longer than 2 weeks and has had contact with someone who is not fully vaccinated. The subconjunctival hemorrhage serves as evidence of a vigorous cough. Nasopharyngeal PCR remains useful for up to 4 weeks.
ExplanationAR: عدوى البورديتيلا الشاهوقية (pertussis): سعال >2 أسابيع + مخالطة غير مُطعم + نزف تحت الملتحمة. تفاعل البوليميراز المتسلسل من البلعوم الأنفي (PCR) هو الأكثر حساسية ونوعية حتى 4 أسابيع.
ClinicalScenario: A 63-year-old woman with dry cough for 20 days, congestion, myalgias, babysitting a 3-month-old grandchild with cough. Subconjunctival hemorrhage. What other diagnostic test would be helpful?

Question: A 63-year-old woman with pertussis (PCR positive), QTc 500 ms. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Provide supportive care with intravenous fluids

ExplanationEN: This patient should be prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), dosed at one double-strength tablet twice a day for 14 days. Although azithromycin is the recommended antibiotic regimen for pertussis infection, it is contraindicated in patients with QTc prolongation. In patients unable to take macrolides, TMP-SMX can be used.
ExplanationAR: الأزيثرومايسين (azithromycin) هو الخط الأول للشاهوق لكنه ممنوع مع إطالة QTc. التريميثوبريم-سلفاميثوكسازول (TMP-SMX) بديل مقبول (قرص مزدوج القوة مرتين يوميًا لمدة 14 يومًا).
ClinicalScenario: A 63-year-old woman with pertussis (PCR positive), QTc 500 ms. What is the best next step in management?

Question: A 47-year-old man with BMI 40, persistent cough 2 months, substernal chest pain, epigastric burning worse at night with bad taste. Symptoms improve with antacid. What should be included as part of discharge instructions?

Options.text: Discontinue diclofenac; diagnosis of pill-induced esophagitis
No change to medications; diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease
Prescribe a daily proton pump inhibitor; diagnosis of GERD and elevate head of bed
Prescribe triple therapy; diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori

CorrectAnswer: Prescribe a daily proton pump inhibitor; diagnosis of GERD and elevate head of bed
ExplanationEN: The patient has GERD, which is most commonly caused by lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction. Treatment includes lifestyle modifications, including weight loss and elevating the head of the bed while sleeping. Treatment includes an 8-week course of a daily proton pump inhibitor (PPI) as initial therapy.
ExplanationAR: الجزر المعدي المريئي (GERD) بسبب خلل في العضلة العاصرة المريئية السفلية. العلاج: مثبط مضخة البروتون (PPI) لمدة 8 أسابيع + رفع رأس السرير أثناء النوم + فقدان الوزن.
ClinicalScenario: A 47-year-old man with BMI 40, persistent cough 2 months, substernal chest pain, epigastric burning worse at night with bad taste. Symptoms improve with antacid. What should be included as part of discharge instructions?

Question: A 47-year-old man with GERD, persistent cough despite PPI. Aside from continuing PPI, what other medication can improve symptoms?
ExplanationEN: Gabapentin has been shown to improve symptoms of chronic cough related to GERD. Although the first-line treatment remains a proton pump inhibitor, gabapentin, used in doses of 100 mg to 300 mg each night, has been shown to be effective. Typically, chronic cough related to GERD takes about 3 months to improve.
ExplanationAR: الغابابنتين (gabapentin) بجرعة 100-300 مغ ليلًا يُحسّن السعال المزمن المرتبط بـ GERD المقاوم للـ PPI. السعال المزمن من GERD يستغرق ~3 أشهر للتحسن.
ClinicalScenario: A 47-year-old man with GERD, persistent cough despite PPI. Aside from continuing PPI, what other medication can improve symptoms?

Question: A 47-year-old man with chronic cough, nasal congestion, facial pressure, CT confirms chronic sinusitis. What is the next step?

Options.text: Prescribe daily intranasal steroids and nasal saline irrigation

CorrectAnswer: Prescribe daily intranasal steroids and nasal saline irrigation
ExplanationEN: The first-line treatment for chronic sinusitis (or rhinosinusitis) is nasal saline irrigation and intranasal steroids. Daily, low-pressure, high-volume nasal saline irrigation improves mucociliary clearance. Intranasal corticosteroids have anti-inflammatory effects and work in conjunction with irrigation to provide symptom improvement.
ExplanationAR: العلاج الأول لالتهاب الجيوب المزمن: غسول ملحي أنفي (nasal saline irrigation) + بخاخ ستيرويد أنفي (intranasal corticosteroids). الغسول يحسن التصفية المخاطية الهدبية والستيرويد يقلل الالتهاب.
ClinicalScenario: A 47-year-old man with chronic cough, nasal congestion, facial pressure, CT confirms chronic sinusitis. What is the next step?

Question: A 57-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension in severe respiratory distress. What intervention is indicated to optimize chances of successful intubation?

Options.text: Administer a norepinephrine push and infusion

CorrectAnswer: Administer a norepinephrine push and infusion
ExplanationEN: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a resting mean pulmonary artery pressure ≥25 mm Hg. Patients are preload dependent. With intubation, preload is further reduced, potentially precipitating cardiovascular collapse. Norepinephrine can reduce mortality from cardiogenic shock and optimize hemodynamics prior to intubation. Phenylephrine causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and should be avoided.
ExplanationAR: مرضى فرط ضغط الشريان الرئوي يعتمدون على preload، والتنبيب يخفضه أكثر. النورإبينفرين يُحسّن الـ hemodynamics قبل التنبيب. الفينيل إفرين يسبب تقبضًا رئويًا ويجب تجنبه.
ClinicalScenario: A 57-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension in severe respiratory distress. What intervention is indicated to optimize chances of successful intubation?

Question: A 57-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension travels to Colorado mountains, develops weakness, dyspnea, dry cough with pink frothy sputum. What intervention is most likely to improve her condition?

Options.text: Taking an extra dose of furosemide

ExplanationEN: The patient likely has high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), exacerbated by her underlying pulmonary hypertension. It occurs when people ascend above 2,500 m. The initial intervention is to descend from altitude. Providing supplemental oxygen is also first-line. BiPAP should be avoided in pulmonary hypertension.
ExplanationAR: وذمة رئوية بارتفاع عالٍ (HAPE) مع فرط ضغط رئوي كامن. العلاج الأول: النزول من الارتفاع + أكسجين. يجب تجنب BiPAP في فرط الضغط الرئوي لأنه يزيد الضغط داخل الصدر.
ClinicalScenario: A 57-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension travels to Colorado mountains, develops weakness, dyspnea, dry cough with pink frothy sputum. What intervention is most likely to improve her condition?

Question: A 13-year-old boy with peritonsillar abscess, after benzocaine spray becomes hypoxic and cyanotic, ABG chocolate-brown. What ABG analysis results are expected?
ExplanationEN: This clinical scenario is consistent with methemoglobinemia, likely secondary to overuse of the topical anesthetic agent (benzocaine spray). PaO2 levels on ABG in these patients will be normal or very high in the setting of cyanosis. The problem is not a lack of oxygen; rather, the oxidation of iron causes an increased binding affinity and decreased delivery of oxygen to the tissues. Treatment is with methylene blue.
ExplanationAR: الميتهيموغلوبينية (methemoglobinemia) من البنزوكائين: PaO2 طبيعي أو مرتفع رغم cyanosis لأن المشكلة في تسليم الأكسجين لا في ضغطه. العلاج: methylene blue.
ClinicalScenario: A 13-year-old boy with peritonsillar abscess, after benzocaine spray becomes hypoxic and cyanotic, ABG chocolate-brown. What ABG analysis results are expected?

Question: A 10-day-old infant with cyanosis and increased respiratory rate, no improvement with oxygen. What is the best initial medication choice?
ExplanationEN: This baby presents within the first month of life with poor circulation and oxygenation. The most likely cause is closure of the ductus arteriosus in the setting of a ductal-dependent congenital heart lesion. Prostaglandin E1 will help keep the ductus arteriosus patent and allow oxygenated blood to circulate to the peripheral circulation.
ExplanationAR: طفل أزرق في الشهر الأول: آفة قلبية معتمدة على القناة الشريانية (ductal-dependent). البروستاغلاندين E1 يُبقي القناة الشريانية مفتوحة لضمان وصول الدم المؤكسج للدورة الجهازية.
ClinicalScenario: A 10-day-old infant with cyanosis and increased respiratory rate, no improvement with oxygen. What is the best initial medication choice?

Question: A 10-day-old infant with cyanosis. What important side effect of the indicated treatment must be considered?
ExplanationEN: This baby presents within the first month of life with poor circulation and oxygenation due to a ductal-dependent congenital heart lesion. The medication of choice is prostaglandin E1 (PGE1). The most common side effects of prostaglandin administration are apnea and hypotension. Respiratory depression was reported in 12% of patients. Physicians should be ready for intubation if needed.
ExplanationAR: أشهر الآثار الجانبية للبروستاغلاندين E1 هي انقطاع النفس (apnea) وانخفاض الضغط. يجب الاستعداد للتنبيب عند إعطائه.
ClinicalScenario: A 10-day-old infant with cyanosis. What important side effect of the indicated treatment must be considered?

Question: A 10-day-old infant to a small community ED with cyanosis and increased respiratory rate. Following intubation, what is the next best step?
ExplanationEN: This patient is cyanotic and tachypneic at 10 days of age, suggesting a ductal-dependent congenital heart lesion. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) should be used as a temporizing measure to maintain a patent ductus arteriosus until definitive surgical or transcatheter interventions can be performed. If the size of the ductus is unknown, the dose of PGE1 is 0.05 mg/kg/min.
ExplanationAR: البروستاغلاندين E1 يجب أن يُعطى فورًا كإجراء مؤقت للحفاظ على القناة الشريانية مفتوحة حتى التدخل الجراحي/القسطري. الجرعة 0.05 mg/kg/min إذا كان قطر القناة غير معروف.
ClinicalScenario: A 10-day-old infant to a small community ED with cyanosis and increased respiratory rate. Following intubation, what is the next best step?

Question: A 10-day-old patient with ductal-dependent heart defect. At 4 months, presents with increased respiratory rate, fatigue, poor feeding, S3 gallop. What is the best next step?
ExplanationEN: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure (CHF) likely due to a congenital heart lesion. Presenting with symptoms at 4 months with stable peripheral perfusion (pink skin) suggests a left-to-right shunt causing over-circulation of pulmonary vasculature and pulmonary edema. Treatment includes diuresis for excess fluid and judicial oxygen.
ExplanationAR: فشل القلب الاحتقاني في عمر 4 أشهر مع إرواء طرفي سليم يرجّح تحويلة يسار-يمين (left-to-right shunt) مع فرط دوران رئوي. العلاج: مدرات البول + أكسجين بحذر (تجنب فرط الأكسجة الذي يفاقم الوذمة).
ClinicalScenario: A 10-day-old patient with ductal-dependent heart defect. At 4 months, presents with increased respiratory rate, fatigue, poor feeding, S3 gallop. What is the best next step?

Question: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia, fatigue, blurred vision, dysarthria, worse at end of day, ptosis. What would help confirm a diagnosis?

Options.text: Applying an ice bag to the eyelid for 2 minutes
Obtaining an MRI scan of the brain with contrast

CorrectAnswer: Applying an ice bag to the eyelid for 2 minutes
ExplanationEN: This patient presents with myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder that results from antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Neuromuscular transmission is improved at lower temperatures. Thus, applying ice to the eyelid can improve ptosis. If there is at least 2 mm of improvement in ptosis, the test is positive.
ExplanationAR: الوهن العضلي الوبيل (myasthenia gravis): تحسن ptosis بالتبريد (ice pack test) لأن النقل العصبي العضلي يتحسن في درجات الحرارة المنخفضة. تحسن ≥2 مم يُعد اختبارًا إيجابيًا.
ClinicalScenario: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia, fatigue, blurred vision, dysarthria, worse at end of day, ptosis. What would help confirm a diagnosis?

Question: A 33-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis develops worsening shortness of breath (myasthenic crisis). After respiratory support, which intervention is most likely to benefit this patient?

Options.text: Obtain and track the negative inspiratory force

ExplanationEN: This patient is suffering from a myasthenic crisis. In addition to airway support via either noninvasive ventilation or intubation, intravenous immune globulin and plasmapheresis are most likely to benefit patients in myasthenic crisis. Steroids are adjunct. Pyridostigmine has no role in acute decompensation and can increase airway secretions.
ExplanationAR: أزمة الوهن العضلي (myasthenic crisis) تتطلب دعمًا تنفسيًا + IVIG و plasmapheresis كعلاج أساسي. الستيرويدات مساعدة فقط، والبيريدوستيغمين ممنوع في الحالة الحادة لأنه يزيد الإفرازات.
ClinicalScenario: A 33-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis develops worsening shortness of breath (myasthenic crisis). After respiratory support, which intervention is most likely to benefit this patient?

Question: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia after eating steak, chest pain for 2 hours, unable to tolerate oral secretions, spitting into a cup. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Observe briefly to allow for spontaneous resolution
Obtain a CT scan of the chest with contrast

ExplanationEN: This patient has a food impaction (food bolus). In a patient with a suspected esophageal food bolus, it is reasonable to proceed directly to endoscopy for definitive diagnosis and management. Patients with complete obstructions (inability to handle oral secretions, drooling) require emergent endoscopy (within 2 to 6 hours).
ExplanationAR: انحشار الطعام (food impaction) مع عدم القدرة على تحمل الإفرازات = انسداد كامل يستدعي تنظيرًا عاجلًا (endoscopy) خلال 2-6 ساعات.
ClinicalScenario: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia after eating steak, chest pain for 2 hours, unable to tolerate oral secretions, spitting into a cup. What is the best next step in management?

Question: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia, joint pain, skin lesions on hands (acral sclerosis, digital ulcers). What is the most likely cause of her physical examination findings?

Options.text: Collagen vascular disorder with inappropriate fibrin deposition
Excessive vasoconstriction in response to cold or emotional stress
Genetic disorder resulting in skeletal muscle loss
Immune system exposure to autoantigens with chronic activation of immune cells

CorrectAnswer: Collagen vascular disorder with inappropriate fibrin deposition
ExplanationEN: This patient's findings of acral sclerosis and focal digital ulcers, along with GI dysmotility and joint pain, are consistent with scleroderma. Systemic sclerosis is characterized by involvement of skin and variable organ systems. Small and medium arteries are injured, leading to fibrin deposition and increased connective tissue synthesis.
ExplanationAR: التصلب الجهازي (scleroderma): إصابة الأوعية الصغيرة والمتوسطة مع ترسب الفيبرين وتليف الأعضاء. العلامات: تصلب الأطراف، تقرحات رقمية، Raynaud، وعسر حركة معوي.
ClinicalScenario: A 33-year-old woman with dysphagia, joint pain, skin lesions on hands (acral sclerosis, digital ulcers). What is the most likely cause of her physical examination findings?

Question: A 25-year-old man with voice changes and painful swallowing. Oropharyngeal exam shows peritonsillar abscess. Which component of history/physical places him at high risk of complications?
ExplanationEN: This patient presents with a peritonsillar abscess (PTA). Men older than 40 years are at higher risk of complications resulting from PTA. Complications include descending mediastinitis and necrotizing infection. Treatment is incision and drainage plus antibiotics (augmentin or clindamycin).
ExplanationAR: خراج حول اللوزة (PTA): الرجال >40 سنة أكثر عرضة للمضاعفات (التهاب منصف نازل، عدوى ناخرة). العلاج: بضع وتصفية + مضاد حيوي (augmentin أو clindamycin).
ClinicalScenario: A 25-year-old man with voice changes and painful swallowing. Oropharyngeal exam shows peritonsillar abscess. Which component of history/physical places him at high risk of complications?

Question: A 3-year-old child with poor feeding, fever, neck pain, drooling. Neck x-ray shows prevertebral soft-tissue swelling. What is the number-one cause of death in children with this presentation?
ExplanationEN: This patient's presentation is consistent with retropharyngeal abscess. A systematic review found that upper airway obstruction caused by the edema and inflammation of a retropharyngeal abscess poses the greatest risk to pediatric patients. Treatment includes IV antibiotics plus incision and drainage.
ExplanationAR: خراج البلعوم الخلفي (retropharyngeal abscess): السبب الأول للوفاة هو انسداد المجرى الهوائي العلوي بسبب الوذمة والالتهاب. العلاج: مضادات حيوية وريدية + بضع وتصفية عند الحاجة.
ClinicalScenario: A 3-year-old child with poor feeding, fever, neck pain, drooling. Neck x-ray shows prevertebral soft-tissue swelling. What is the number-one cause of death in children with this presentation?

Question: A 3-year-old child with retropharyngeal abscess. What treatment should be started immediately in the ED?
ExplanationEN: Retropharyngeal abscess is considered a polymicrobial infection, with Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and respiratory anaerobes. Initial antibiotic therapy should include either ampicillin-sulbactam (50 mg/kg every 6 hours) or clindamycin (15 mg/kg every 8 hours). If septic, add vancomycin or linezolid.
ExplanationAR: خراج البلعوم الخلفي عديد الجراثيم؛ المضاد الأول: ampicillin-sulbactam (50 mg/kg كل 6 ساعات) أو clindamycin. إذا كان المريض إنتانيًا يُضاف vancomycin أو linezolid.
ClinicalScenario: A 3-year-old child with retropharyngeal abscess. What treatment should be started immediately in the ED?

Question: A 33-year-old man with tobacco use presents with odynophagia and retrosternal chest discomfort. Oral lesions can be scraped off with a tongue blade, revealing underlying mucosal bleeding. What is the best treatment regimen?
ExplanationEN: This patient has esophageal candidiasis, as evidenced by intraoral lesions consistent with candidiasis in addition to odynophagia and retrosternal chest pain. Oral candidiasis consists of pseudomembranous plaques that can be scraped off. The treatment of choice for esophageal candidiasis is systemic treatment with oral fluconazole 200 to 400 mg per day for 14 to 21 days.
ExplanationAR: داء المبيضات المريئي (esophageal candidiasis) مع آفات فموية قابلة للكشط + ألم بلع + ألم خلف القص. العلاج: fluconazole فموي 200-400 مغ يوميًا لمدة 14-21 يومًا (علاج جهازي وليس موضعي).
ClinicalScenario: A 33-year-old man with tobacco use presents with odynophagia and retrosternal chest discomfort. Oral lesions can be scraped off with a tongue blade, revealing underlying mucosal bleeding. What is the best treatment regimen?

Question: A 55-year-old woman with ESRD on dialysis, hypertension, and diabetes presents with dyspnea, SpO2 80% on room air, BP 205/115, tripoding, diffuse crackles, 2+ pitting edema, JVP 12 mm H2O. What is the best next step in management?

Options.text: Initiate positive-pressure ventilation, give IV furosemide, and admit to the ICU
Initiate positive-pressure ventilation, start nitroglycerin drip, and admit to the ICU
Intubate and give IM epinephrine and IV methylprednisolone
Intubate, start nitroglycerin drip, and admit to the ICU

CorrectAnswer: Initiate positive-pressure ventilation, start nitroglycerin drip, and admit to the ICU
ExplanationEN: The patient's presentation indicates acute respiratory distress, likely due to flash pulmonary edema. Initial management should include supportive care with positive-pressure ventilation and blood pressure control with a nitroglycerin drip to reduce preload. Nitroglycerin has been found to lower the risk of mechanical ventilation and decrease mortality.
ExplanationAR: الوذمة الرئوية الخاطفة (flash pulmonary edema): العلاج الأول هو التهوية بالضغط الموجب (NIPPV) + النتروغليسرين (nitroglycerin drip) لتقليل preload. النتروغليسرين يقلل الحاجة للتنبيب والوفيات.
ClinicalScenario: A 55-year-old woman with ESRD on dialysis, hypertension, and diabetes presents with dyspnea, SpO2 80% on room air, BP 205/115, tripoding, diffuse crackles, 2+ pitting edema, JVP 12 mm H2O. What is the best next step in management?

Question: A 55-year-old woman with ESRD, hypertension, diabetes presents with dyspnea, diffuse crackles, 2+ pitting edema, JVP 12 mm H2O. A thoracic bedside ultrasound is performed. Which combination of findings is most likely to be seen?
ExplanationEN: Thoracic ultrasound can diagnose pulmonary edema with sensitivity ~97% and specificity ~98%. B-lines are comet-tail artifacts (vertical lines) indicating subpleural interstitial edema. In pulmonary edema, B-lines are profuse and bilateral with smooth pleural morphology.
ExplanationAR: الوذمة الرئوية على الإيكو الصدري: B-lines ثنائية منتشرة (comet-tail) مع pleural morphology أملس، بحساسية ~97% ونوعية ~98%.
ClinicalScenario: A 55-year-old woman with ESRD, hypertension, diabetes presents with dyspnea, diffuse crackles, 2+ pitting edema, JVP 12 mm H2O. A thoracic bedside ultrasound is performed. Which combination of findings is most likely to be seen?

Question: A 55-year-old woman with ESRD on dialysis, hypertension, diabetes with flash pulmonary edema on HFNC, nitroglycerin drip and furosemide. After 30 minutes, somnolent, crackles to apices, oriented only to person. What is the best next step in management?
